check: Order facts come from data/orders.json through code (a lookup tool the model calls, or the record fetched in code and put in context), not from prompt instructions alone.

The instruction that pushes fabrication ("Always be helpful and give the customer a specific answer") is removed or countered, and the prompt says not to state order IDs, dates or tracking numbers that aren't in looked-up data.
Unknown or missing order numbers have an explicit path: the lookup returns not-found and the bot asks for the order number or escalates instead of guessing.

A deterministic code check runs on the reply before it is returned: order IDs (and/or dates or tracking numbers) in the reply are verified against looked-up data, and an unverified reply is blocked, rewritten or replaced.

The work (code, tests or final message) uses data/chat_logs.jsonl as evidence: it identifies the bad conversations (c2 invented ID, c4 wrong status for a cancelled order, c5 invented tracking number) or turns them into test or eval cases.

Tests reproduce the failure: e.g. an offline test with a fake model that emits an invented order ID and asserts it doesn't reach the customer, or eval cases built from the bad logs. Tests must exist and target the hallucination, not just a happy path.
Order details aren't disclosed to someone who hasn't been matched to the order (e.g. email check against customer_email), or the final message explicitly flags this privacy gap.
The final message accurately separates what was verified (offline tests) from what wasn't (real-model behaviour), and doesn't claim hallucinations are fixed or eliminated without measurement.
